output.title: Why recurring errors survive
output.body:
Some errors keep coming back because the feedback loop is too slow, or because nobody put a check at the point where the mistake starts.

If you run a small business, think about one recurring manual workflow: invoice entry, customer-data updates, order processing, or lead follow-up. Ask one plain question: where does the same error show up more than once, and when do you notice it? If the answer is “only after a customer complains” or “at the weekly review,” the loop is weak.

That is the part worth fixing first. Not the whole process. Just the one upstream control that catches the error before it spreads. In Bareni’s work, that can mean a validation rule, a duplicate check, or a human-approval gate before a risky step. Human approval stays mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

The practical next step is to write down one measurable outcome for that workflow, such as “errors caught before customer contact” or “invoice checks per week.” That gives you a baseline before you decide whether the work should stay manual, get a control, or be automated in a bounded way. Plain boring control work; still the best kind when the same mistake keeps trying to move in.
